subject: maths
title: The 2, 5 and 10 Times Tables
seo_title: Year 2 Times Tables Worksheets: 2, 5 and 10 Times Tables, Odd and Even
standard_text: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers.
meta_desc: Free Year 2 maths worksheets on the 2, 5 and 10 times tables: equal groups, counting in 2s, 5s and 10s with coins and clocks, odd and even numbers, division facts and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, following the National Curriculum.
key_big: Count in 2s, 5s and 10s. Every answer in the 2 times table is even.
key_sub: 3 × 5 means 3 groups of 5: 5, 10, 15. Odd or even? Look at the ones digit only. Each fact gives a division fact too: 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
body_html:
Multiplication is equal groups

3 × 5 means 3 groups of 5. Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15. So 3 × 5 = 15. You can swap the numbers: 5 × 3 = 15 too.

Count in 2s, 5s and 10s

The 2 times table is doubles: 2 × 7 = 7 + 7 = 14. The 5 times table ends in 0 or 5, like 5p coins and the minutes on a clock. The 10 times table ends in 0, like 10p coins.

Odd and even numbers

Put the objects in pairs. If none are left over, the number is even. If 1 is left over, it is odd. For a big number, look at the ones digit only: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

Example

5 × 7 = ?

Count in 5s, 7 times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35.

Answer: 35

Division

20 ÷ 2 = ?

Division is the inverse of multiplication. Think: 2 × ? = 20. 2 × 10 = 20.

Answer: 10

Word problem

How many 10p coins make 60p?

Count in 10s: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. That is 6 tens.

Answer: 6 coins

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding instead: 5 × 3 = 8× means groups of: 3 groups of 5 = 15
One group too many: 5 × 6 = 35Count in 5s carefully: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
Saying 43 is even because 4 is evenLook at the ones digit: 43 ends in 3, so it is odd
Giving the big number in division: 20 ÷ 2 = 20Ask: 2 times what makes 20? The answer is 10

faq.q: What times tables do Year 2 children learn?
faq.a: The 2, 5 and 10 times tables. The National Curriculum says Year 2 pupils should recall and use the multiplication and division facts for these tables, and recognise odd and even numbers.

faq.q: How do you know if a number is odd or even?
faq.a: Look at the ones digit. If it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 the number is even; if it is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 it is odd. So 41 is odd, even though it has 4 tens.

faq.q: How can I help my child learn the 2, 5 and 10 times tables?
faq.a: Count in 2s, 5s and 10s out loud, then use real things: pairs of socks, 5p and 10p coins, and the minutes on a clock. A few minutes of practice each day works better than one long session.

faq.q: Which times tables come after Year 2?
faq.a: In Year 3 children learn the 3, 4 and 8 times tables. By the end of Year 4 they should know every table up to 12 × 12 for the Multiplication Tables Check.

items.q: The red hand is the minute hand. How many minutes past 3 is it?
items.e: The minute hand points to 4. Each number on the clock is 5 minutes. Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. So it is 20 minutes past 3.

items.q: Which number is in the 2, the 5 and the 10 times tables?
items.e: 30 ends in 0, so it is in all three: 2 × 15, 5 × 6 and 10 × 3. 25 and 15 are only in the 5 times table. 12 is only in the 2 times table.

items.q: Which digit tells you if a number is odd or even?
items.e: Only the ones digit matters. 41 has 4 tens, but it ends in 1, so 41 is odd.

items.q: What is the next even number after 36?
items.e: Even numbers go up in 2s: 36, 38. 37 is the next number, but it is odd.

items.q: What is the next odd number after 47?
items.e: Odd numbers go up in 2s: 47, 49. 48 is the next number, but it is even.

items.e: Each number is 2 more: 7 + 2 = 9. These are the odd numbers.

items.q: Which list has only even numbers?
items.e: 12, 14, 16 all end in 2, 4 or 6. 21, 41, 61 have even tens digits, but they end in 1, so they are odd.

items.q: Harry has 9 pairs of gloves. How many gloves? Odd or even?
items.e: A pair is 2. 9 × 2 = 18. Every glove has a partner, so 18 is even. 11 is 9 + 2, which adds instead of multiplies.

items.q: There are 17 children in a class. They work in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
items.e: 17 is odd, because it ends in 7. 8 pairs make 16, so 1 child is left over.

items.q: There are 28 pupils in a class. They work in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
items.e: 28 ends in 8, so it is even. 14 pairs make 28. Nobody is left over.

items.q: 15 counters are put into groups of 5. How many groups?
items.e: Count the groups: there are 3. 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Check: 3 × 5 = 15.

items.q: Ruby shares 12 strawberries equally between 2 bowls. How many go in each bowl?
items.e: 12 ÷ 2 = ? Half of 12 is 6. Check: 2 × 6 = 12. So 6 strawberries.

items.e: 30 ÷ 5 = ? Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. That is 6 fives, so 6 teams.

items.e: 70 ÷ 10 = ? 7 tens make 70. So 7 coins.

items.q: A duck has 2 legs. How many legs do 9 ducks have?

items.e: 50 ÷ 10 = ? 5 tens make 50. So there are 5 towers.

items.q: Leo puts 40 biscuits on plates, 5 on each plate. How many plates does he need?
items.e: 40 ÷ 5 = ? 5 × 8 = 40, so he needs 8 plates.

items.q: Grace has three 10p coins and four 5p coins. How much money does she have?
items.e: Three 10p coins: 10, 20, 30. Four 5p coins: 5, 10, 15, 20. 30p + 20p = 50p. 7p counts the coins, not the money.

items.q: Isla shares 20 stickers equally with a friend. How many does each child get?
items.e: Sharing between 2 children: 20 ÷ 2 = 10. Check: 2 × 10 = 20. Each child gets 10 stickers.
